newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS-POLAND PLANS ZLOTY LIBERALISATION IN 1998.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-POLAND PLANS ZLOTY LIBERALISATION IN 1998.

text.p: Poland plans to bring its zloty another step nearer full convertibility next year but also wants a new currency law to give control over short-term capital flows, a senior central banker said on Friday.

Michal Krakowiak, head of the National Bank of Poland's currency department, told a banking seminar in Stara Wies outside Warsaw, that a new currency law planned for early 1998 would make the zloty externally convertible.
"The law will establish the principle that the zloty can be used as settlement currency outside Poland," Krakowiak said.
The zloty can now be used as a means of settlement only inside Poland although it can be freely exchanged for other currencies.

Krakowiak said the bill, prepared by the finance ministry and the central bank, would also increase to the status of a law an existing regulation that frees currency accounts and capital flows in line with Poland's OECD entry agreement.
"We introduce a general rule that there is freedom in current account transfers and capital flows," he said.
Krakowiak said the bill would probably include a so-called negative list of types of capital transactions that would still require central bank approval.
He said further liberalisations would be made gradually in line with a tentative timetable agreed with the OECD.
But he said the central bank wanted the new law to give monetary authorities special powers to put temporary restrictions on flows of short-term capital, especially in government securities.
"Along with a liberalisation (of currency flows) we also want to have parallel regulations permitting, in speical situations, to limit access of short-term capital," he said.
He said such restrictions could, for example, apply to transfers of profits abroad rather than entry by foreign speculators into Polish securities.
Krakowiak said Poland planned to allow free transfer of funds abroad from non-public securities issues in Poland in 1999. Poland already allows such transfers for public issues.
He also said Polish citizens, who are now allowed to invest in OECD long-term debt securities and stocks, would be allowed to buy short-term money market instruments also from 1999.
But he said Poland would probably wait until after the year 2002 before allowing Poles to keep their savings abroad, which would remove the last obstacle to full zloty convertibility.
Krakowiak said that the central bank preferred to move gradually to full zloty convertibility because Poland's high foreign debt and current account deficit called for caution.
He said that even though Poland's official reserves now remained relatively high at about $18 billion, the country faced an expected increase in costs of debt repayments and financing in the future.
